profile.name: Martin Ignacio Zangl
profile.headline: Senior Android Engineer
profile.summary: I build and stabilize Android products, most recently payment SDKs and an offline-first clinical app. When the work crosses a platform boundary, I follow it into React Native, Flutter, iOS, or Java services.
longSummary: I have spent 12+ years building Android products and 15+ years in software. Recent work includes payment SDKs at Checkout.com and reliability work on Swift Medical's offline-first clinical app.

At Swift Medical, synchronization and memory changes helped move crash-free usage from about 70% to 99.6%. At PayPal and MercadoLibre, I worked on financial journeys that crossed mobile apps, testing, release trains, and Java middle-end services.
I still write product code. I also mentor developers, review Android candidates, and share what I learn through internal sessions and community talks.

work.summary: Published the Android Payment Flow sample, resolved recurring React Native SDK crashes, and shipped two releases across its Android and iOS dependencies.
achievements: Finished and published the public Jetpack Compose sample as working integration code for merchants, using the iOS sample as the UI and UX reference.
Took over the React Native SDK until a specialist joined, resolved recurring crashes, and shipped two releases with changes to the Android and iOS dependencies.
Added co-branded card support to close a feature gap with the web SDK, working directly with merchants to trace and prioritize integration issues.
Documented differences in configuration, styling, and behavior between the Android and iOS SDKs, and worked on internal tooling for configuring and running the sample app.
outcomes: The public Android sample gave merchants a complete Jetpack Compose integration they could run and inspect.
Recurring React Native crashes stopped and two releases shipped with the required native dependency changes.
Android gained co-branded card support as part of the planned work toward parity with the web SDK.

story.title: Shipping fixes across three payment SDKs
story.context: Checkout.com brought me into the Android Payment Flow team through Parser. I started by finishing the public Android sample, then took over the React Native SDK until a specialist joined.
story.challenge: Merchants were reporting recurring React Native crashes. Fixing them meant tracing behavior through the wrapper and its Android and iOS dependencies, then coordinating releases in the right order.
decisions: I followed each issue into the native SDK that owned the behavior instead of treating the React Native wrapper as an isolated codebase.
I used the existing iOS sample as the UI and UX reference for Android and documented the platform differences I found while building the Jetpack Compose version.
Merchant reports set the order of the work. I joined customer calls, reproduced integration problems, and kept the teams aligned while fixes moved toward release.
quality: Compared configuration, styling, and behavior across Android and iOS while implementing the public sample.
Verified the React Native fixes against updated Android and iOS dependencies before each release.
Kept the developer tooling separate from merchant code while simplifying how the team configured and ran the sample app.

work.summary: Recovered documents that had been stuck on devices for months and improved stability through synchronization and memory changes.
achievements: Moved synchronization state out of WorkManager and into an application-owned queue that preserved document order.
Compared memory and CPU behavior in a low-priority Coroutines pilot before migrating the remaining synchronization work.
Used Android Profiler and Perfetto to trace long-session leaks to bitmap handling and encryption work that blocked threads.
Identified production performance problems during a limited analytics rollout and paused the release until the internal library was fixed.
Supported native camera plugins on Android and iOS, enabled ARM64 simulator support for OpenCV and TensorFlow, and migrated C++ dependencies for 16 KB memory pages.
outcomes: Documents that had been waiting on customer devices for months successfully synchronized.
The application gained explicit synchronization queue ownership and better processing observability.
SwiftVision shipped with ARM64 iOS Simulator support, and native-library support for 16 KB pages was delivered by the required deadline.

story.title: Recovering months of stalled document sync
story.context: Swift Medical's clinical Android app had to create documents and capture images without a reliable network. I later moved to its Flutter product and handled native Android and iOS work around the camera and computer-vision stack.
story.challenge: Failed synchronization was the main customer complaint. Pending work was coupled to WorkManager's internal state, and out-of-order operations were rejected by the backend. Some documents remained on devices for months. Long sessions also exposed memory leaks and expensive bitmap and encryption work.
decisions: The product needed to own synchronization state and ordering. WorkManager continued to schedule execution, while the application database held pending domain operations.
A measured pilot established whether Coroutines improved the existing thread-heavy implementation before extending the change. I moved the busiest flows first instead of rewriting everything at once.
Production behavior determined whether the analytics replacement was ready. I paused the first limited rollout, fixed the internal library with the team, and resumed the release.
quality: Used CPU and Memory Profilers, allocation and leak analysis, and Perfetto to investigate long-session failures and blocked threads.
Compared resource use before expanding the synchronization migration and monitored adoption and performance during analytics rollout.
Compiled OpenCV and TensorFlow dependencies for ARM64 iOS simulators and validated SwiftVision with the computer-vision team before its production release.

work.summary: Built repeatable tests for complete Savings journeys, exposed a stale balance defect, and owned Credits UK module integration in release trains.
achievements: Mapped the Savings journey and documented existing behavior before planning small refactors.
Introduced integration and end-to-end validation alongside existing unit tests.
Built a test library to inject and queue backend responses, including edge cases, with Page Objects for reusable customer journeys.
Restructured functional flows with MVVM and unidirectional data flow and worked with DevOps on Jenkins coverage reporting.
Owned module release integration and coordinated fixes for cross-module conflicts.
outcomes: Exposed and reproduced an incorrect balance that previously required a manual refresh, protecting corrected behavior with automation.
Established reusable scenarios for full financial journeys.
Resolved a cross-module theme conflict before it delayed feature integration.

story.title: Reproducing complete financial journeys
story.context: I joined PayPal Savings while it was live as an MVP. Its customer journey covered compliance, activation, balances, and funding sources. I later moved to Credits UK, contributing across Android, iOS, and Java services.
story.challenge: Strong unit coverage did not establish that complete customer journeys worked across module, API, and UI boundaries. One business-rule defect displayed an incorrect balance until the customer refreshed.
decisions: Incremental refactoring preserved verified behavior in a live financial product while allowing delivery to continue.

Explicit event-to-state paths made asynchronous compliance, funding, and balance operations easier to trace. Reproducible backend responses connected a visible balance inconsistency to the underlying business rule.
End-to-end tests broadened confidence but cost more to maintain. Queued responses and Page Objects controlled environment variability and repetitive setup.
quality: Measured coverage across unit, integration, and end-to-end layers in Jenkins.
Reproduced success and failure scenarios with controlled backend responses and verified corrected balance behavior.
Tested the assembled application in release trains. During a theme migration, traced a duplicate dependency to another module and coordinated the correction.

work.summary: Built shared Android resources, an installment-payment journey, and a virtual-card dashboard for the Brazil launch.
achievements: Built a resource SDK that made shared UI components and image resources available across the app.
Built the installment-payment journey and virtual-card dashboard for Brazil. Customers could see available credit, review installment usage, and pay overdue amounts.
Defined contracts between Android and the middle end, then changed its Java and Spark Framework implementation to support both flows.
Built complex server-driven screens with an internal unidirectional data flow framework based on dispatchers and stores.
Defined P50 to P99 latency measures alongside journey completion and payment-timing signals, then worked with architecture on app-wide observability.
outcomes: Delivered resource handling and components intended for consumption across product teams.
Connected mobile payloads, customer events, and telemetry within complete product flows.
Identified release-train edge cases and worked with the architecture team on observability improvements.

story.title: Building credit flows across Android and the middle end
story.context: My first MercadoLibre assignment was a resource SDK for UI components and images shared across the app. I later moved to the virtual credit-card team for the Brazil launch.
story.challenge: The installment-payment journey and card dashboard crossed Android, a Java middle end, shared UI libraries, and a release train used by many teams. Their contracts and state transitions had to stay coherent when the modules came together.
decisions: Feature-specific behavior stayed in its owning module. Shared components needed a clear reuse case because API evolution, compatibility, and governance affected other teams.

Server-driven composition supported flows that benefited from middle-end control. An internal unidirectional data flow framework kept state transitions explicit while the middle end supplied component hierarchy, navigation, and behavior.
Module autonomy made release-train validation essential. Integration edge cases became inputs to shared observability improvements.
quality: Tested module behavior and edge cases against required coverage expectations.
Defined latency percentiles from P50 through P99 alongside customer-journey progression and payment timing signals.
Investigated alerts and weak product metrics with the team, sharing discoveries and clarifying initially incomplete use cases.
